walkthroughs.body_html:
Area of Study 6: Innovations in Music 1900 to Present — a core area of A-Level Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area of Study 6: Innovations in Music 1900 to Present brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area of Study 6: Innovations in Music 1900 to Present.

Did music after 1900 abandon all earlier tradition?
options: Musique concrete means music performed on concrete percussion blocks.
No - many innovators reworked the past: neoclassicism revived eighteenth-century forms, and serialists wrote dance suites and variations.
Twentieth-century composers rejected everything that came before them.
After 1900 composers were forbidden to write for the orchestra.

mcqs.q: Is musique concrete the same as synthesised electronic music?
options: All studio-made music of the 1950s is the same thing: electronic music.
Aleatoric music is created by an audience vote during the concert.
Musique concrete means music performed on concrete percussion blocks.
No - musique concrete manipulates recordings of real-world sounds, whereas elektronische Musik generates sounds electronically from scratch.

mcqs.q: Does aleatoric music let performers do absolutely anything?
options: Aleatoric music is created by an audience vote during the concert.
Musique concrete means music performed on concrete percussion blocks.
No - the composer fixes a framework and leaves specific elements, such as the order of fragments, to chance or choice.
In aleatoric music the performers ignore the score and play freely.
